title: Telephone town-hall participation can improve evaluations of the forum and Member, while deliberative design mainly improves the forum evaluation
source_unit: Abernathy, Esterling, Freebourn, Kennedy, Minozzi, Neblo, and Solis field experiment with Members of Congress
geography: United States congressional districts; four Members of Congress and eight telephone town-hall sessions

observations.period: 2019 publication; fieldwork conducted in congressional districts before publication

denominator.unit: constituents who consented, enrolled, and completed the pretest after recruitment for eight sessions; 222 completed both pretest and posttest

participation_effect.value: attendance at a standard telephone town hall produced statistically significant pre/post improvements in evaluations of the telephone-town-hall platform and the participating Member
participation_effect.unit: reported causal before-after estimate among selected participants

member_trust_approval_change.unit: approximately 4% of the 0-1 response scale for trust and approval

modified_design_effect.unit: approximately 5% of the response scale additional effect on evaluations of the town-hall platform; Cohen's d=0.25

modified_design_member_effect.value: no statistically significant improvement relative to the standard design in attitudes toward Members; estimates were at most small declines of about 0.02 on the 0-1 scale

observations.method: Four Members each hosted one standard telephone town hall and one modified session. The modified session focused on one topic and sent two-page nonpartisan briefing materials beforehand; the standard session followed an open-topic format. Constituents selected which session to attend, and the study estimated pre/post changes plus a difference-in-differences comparison across designs.
observations.uncertainty: The source enrolled 1,005 people but analyzed only 222 pre/post respondents after about 78% attrition. All participating Members were Democrats; only 35 analyzed respondents were Republicans in the reported party subsample. The study lacked a true no-event control, used self-selection into the two sessions, and estimates a local effect for participating Members and constituents rather than a national population effect.
observations.subgroup: Constituents who opted into telephone town halls hosted by four Democratic Members; the study reports larger point estimates among respondents starting below the midpoint of the attitude scales, but those respondents had already agreed to participate.
observations.counterinterpretation: Improved evaluations may reflect attention, familiarity, or demand effects rather than durable institutional legitimacy or policy responsiveness. A better-designed forum improved perceptions of the forum itself without clearly improving perceptions of the Member, separating procedural satisfaction from representative trust.

related_sources.claim: Publisher abstract and metadata identify the article, field-experiment design, and headline findings.

boundary: This record adds a causal communication-design layer between constituent interaction and perceived forum/Member evaluation. It does not establish present-day national prevalence, actual office response, issue resolution, policy influence, durable trust, or equal access to two-way representation.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official Ohio State-hosted paper PDF downloaded and hashed; publisher record cross-checked.
